checkboxes.description: Controllers handle only HTTP layer (req/res) without business logic

evidence.reasoning: ToolsController.getAll() contains significant business logic including query parameter parsing, enum mapping, filter construction, and sort field building across 30+ lines. Controllers should only handle HTTP request/response extraction and delegate all logic to services.
Other controller methods (create, getDetails, update) correctly delegate to service layer without business logic, demonstrating inconsistent implementation within the same controller class.

checkboxes.description: Services layer centralizes business logic and is HTTP-independent

evidence.reasoning: ToolsService.createTool() implements proper business validation by checking category existence before creating tool and throwing NotFoundException with business-appropriate error messages, demonstrating service-layer business logic.

ToolsService.getDetailsById() orchestrates multiple data sources (repository and usageLogs services) and applies business transformations (monthly_cost formatting, usage_metrics aggregation), showing proper service-layer coordination.

Services are HTTP-independent with no imports of HTTP-specific decorators from @nestjs/common (only Injectable, Logger, NotFoundException). Services work with DTOs and domain objects, not Request/Response objects, confirming proper layer independence.

checkboxes.description: Models/Repositories handle only data access (CRUD) without business rules

evidence.reasoning: RepositoryTool.getFiltersWhere() contains business logic with complex conditional filter construction including business rules for min/max cost handling and category name mapping. Repositories should only execute data access operations, not implement business rules.

RepositoryTool.paginatedTools() implements business logic including sort field mapping (SortName.cost to monthly_cost) and pagination calculation. Repository should receive ready-to-use Prisma query objects from service layer, not perform business transformations.

checkboxes.description: No direct database queries in controllers

evidence.reasoning: All controllers delegate to services without any direct database access. No Prisma client imports or database queries found in any controller file. ToolsController consistently calls service methods for all operations.
AppController also follows the pattern of no database queries, only service delegation, confirming consistent application of this principle across all controllers.

rules.reasoning: This NestJS application implements a 3-layer architecture (Controller-Service-Repository) with mixed results. The positive aspects include complete absence of database queries in controllers (all delegate to services) and services that properly centralize business logic with validation, orchestration, and HTTP independence. However, there are two critical violations: (1) ToolsController.getAll contains 30+ lines of business logic for query parsing, enum mapping, and filter construction that should be in the service layer, and (2) Repository classes contain business logic in methods like getFiltersWhere and paginatedTools which implement conditional filtering rules and field mapping instead of pure data access. The architecture foundation is solid but needs refinement to achieve proper separation of concerns, particularly moving business logic from controllers and repositories into the service layer where it belongs.

rules.reasoning: This NestJS TypeScript project demonstrates good junior-level code quality in several areas: descriptive variable names, clear function naming conventions, appropriate function lengths (enforced by ESLint max 50 lines), no dead code, and structured logging with NestJS Logger. However, it falls short in three critical areas: (1) lack of meaningful comments for complex logic like date calculations and filter building, (2) code duplication in cost formatting logic appearing 3 times and repetitive filter copying, and (3) multiple magic values including decimal precision (2), date calculations (1, 30), connection limits (5), and default port (3000) that should be named constants. The codebase scores 11 out of 17 points, showing solid fundamentals but needing improvement in documentation, DRY principles, and constant extraction.
